articles.title: Is unconditional support for Israel becoming a liability for Republicans?
articles.summary: JD Vance’s response to the midterm defeat suggests a once-untouchable Republican consensus may be starting to crack.
articles.body:
The sweeping Republican defeat in the November 3 midterm elections may have opened a debate that, until recently, would have been almost unthinkable within the party: whether the United States should fundamentally reconsider its relationship with Israel.

For decades, unwavering support for Israel was a defining feature of Republican identity, sustained by evangelical Christians, the conservative foreign policy establishment, influential lobbying organisations, and a deeply entrenched congressional consensus. Now, following the electorate’s repudiation of Donald Trump and his administration, that consensus is showing unmistakable signs of strain.

The clearest indication came from Vice President JD Vance, who acknowledged in an unusually candid post-election assessment that dissatisfaction with America’s relationship with Israel was among the reasons Republican voters abandoned their party. Identifying four concerns driving former Trump supporters towards Democrats, Vance cited the Iran war, the cost of living and inflation, the principle of putting America first, and, significantly, changing the American relationship with Israel.

His admission was remarkable not simply because of what he said, but because of who said it. As the administration’s second-highest official and a potential Republican presidential contender in 2028, Vance effectively acknowledged that unconditional support for the Israeli government is no longer politically cost-free, even within the Republican coalition.

More importantly, he brought into the open a question Republican politicians have traditionally been reluctant to entertain: whether America’s commitment to Israel continues to serve America’s own interests.

Does this represent a genuine reassessment, however, or merely an attempt to explain an electoral disaster and reposition the party for 2028?

There are compelling reasons to believe that something more consequential is under way. The Republican alliance with Israel has rested on several overlapping foundations: evangelical Christian support, strategic and intelligence cooperation, military interests, and conservative political organisations that have made backing Israel an almost unquestionable test of political loyalty.

But those foundations are increasingly being challenged by a younger generation of conservatives, particularly within the emerging America First movement, who question why American resources and military commitments should be directed towards foreign conflicts while economic pressures mount at home.

Their scepticism does not necessarily reflect sympathy for Palestinians or opposition to Israel’s existence. Rather, it challenges the assumption that American and Israeli interests are automatically identical. Increasingly, these voters want to know why Washington should continue providing extensive military assistance, diplomatic protection, and political support regardless of the policies pursued by the Israeli government.

The wars in Gaza and Iran have brought that question into sharper focus. Israel’s devastating military campaign in Gaza, the resulting humanitarian catastrophe, and Washington’s continued military and diplomatic backing have imposed mounting moral, diplomatic, and strategic costs on the United States. The subsequent confrontation with Iran further exposed the dangers of allowing Israeli security priorities and regional calculations to influence American decisions about war and peace.

Vance’s intervention, therefore, did not emerge from a political vacuum. It reflects tensions that have been developing within the Republican electorate for years. Earlier polling had already identified declining enthusiasm for Israel among younger Republicans, even as traditional constituencies remained considerably more supportive. The Chicago Council’s 2026 survey also found declining Republican favourability towards Israel compared with 2022, although Republicans continued to favour maintaining or increasing military assistance. The picture is consequently not of a party abandoning Israel, but of one increasingly divided over the terms and consequences of the relationship.

That division could become central to the Republican Party’s struggle over its post-Trump future. By identifying dissatisfaction with Israel policy as a factor in the electoral losses, Vance has effectively legitimised a debate that conservative politicians have long avoided. He has also signalled that the issue could become an important point of differentiation among potential presidential contenders preparing for 2028.

For Trump, the contradiction is particularly damaging. He built his political movement around putting America first and ending costly foreign entanglements, yet his presidency has become closely associated with extraordinary support for Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, including military cooperation, diplomatic backing, and confrontation with regional adversaries.

The Iran war has made that contradiction harder to defend. Voters who supported Trump expecting him to prioritise domestic concerns may reasonably question why the United States became entangled in another Middle Eastern conflict, particularly when the consequences include economic uncertainty, higher energy costs, and resources diverted from domestic priorities.

While Trump has acknowledged that the Iran conflict contributed to Republican losses, he has continued defending the decision to launch it. Vance, meanwhile, has been more explicit in recognising the political price of the administration’s foreign policy choices. That difference could become an important fault line within the Republican leadership.

Yet recognising the political costs of the relationship is not the same as changing it. The institutional forces sustaining the US-Israel alliance remain formidable. Congressional Republicans have traditionally supported substantial military assistance, while evangelical organisations, influential donors, lobbying networks, and defence sector interests continue to exercise considerable influence. Beyond domestic politics, the relationship encompasses intelligence sharing, military technology, regional security arrangements, and decades of diplomatic commitments.

Consequently, even an administration persuaded that unconditional support carries electoral risks could find it difficult to translate that recognition into meaningful policy. Changing the rhetoric is considerably easier than changing military appropriations, arms transfers, diplomatic positions, and the strategic architecture underpinning the alliance.

Nevertheless, the midterm results have altered Washington’s political calculations. With Democrats controlling both chambers of Congress, continued military assistance and diplomatic protection will face greater scrutiny. Republicans contemplating their political future must also consider whether defending every decision of the Israeli government remains electorally advantageous, particularly among younger voters and independents whose support increasingly determines national outcomes.

The real test, therefore, will not be what Republican politicians say in the aftermath of their defeat, but what they are prepared to do. Will they support conditions on military assistance? Reconsider automatic diplomatic protection when Israeli policies violate international law? Challenge settlement expansion and annexationist ambitions? And will they recognise that a sustainable regional settlement must address Palestinian freedom, security, and political rights rather than treating them as secondary considerations?

These are the questions that distinguish a genuine reassessment from electoral opportunism.

For Palestinians, the stakes are considerable. A meaningful Republican shift could create political space for greater accountability, a less permissive American approach to Israeli military operations, and renewed pressure for a political settlement grounded in Palestinian rights. But expectations should remain measured. A change in Republican rhetoric does not necessarily translate into a change in America’s strategic priorities, much less an immediate departure from decades of established policy.

Ultimately, the significance of the midterm defeat may lie less in an immediate transformation of American policy than in the erosion of an assumption that has governed Washington for generations: that support for Israel is politically untouchable. The Republican Party now faces a choice: ignore the warning or recognise that its political future may depend, in part, on responding to it.

The alliance is not about to disappear. But the political immunity that has long shielded it from serious scrutiny may finally be eroding. Whether that erosion produces a substantive change in American policy towards Israel remains the defining question of the post-election period.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Photos: Heavy rains leave tens of thousands without shelter in Gaza
articles.summary: Heavy rain floods tents housing displaced Palestinians in Gaza as Israeli restrictions on aid hamper response.
articles.body:
Heavy rain has flooded tens of thousands of displaced people’s tents in war-devastated Gaza, Palestinian authorities said, leaving many without shelter.

Since early Saturday, displaced families have been seen fleeing camps in parts of Gaza City and other northern areas of the territory, as well as parts of central Gaza, after they were inundated by rainwater.

Gaza authorities said about “70,000 tents sheltering tens of thousands of displaced people were flooded on the first day” of rains.

The statement also noted the “collapse of dozens of cracked walls and roofs, which caused injuries”, some of them critical, in various areas of the war-devastated territory.

Palestinian Civil Defence spokesman Mahmoud Basal told the news agency AFP on Saturday his teams had received more than 1,500 calls during the night from residents requesting urgent assistance after their tents were flooded, explaining that the agency “is operating without any equipment or capabilities”.

“We have issued an urgent distress call to the international community and humanitarian organisations to intervene immediately to save hundreds of thousands of displaced people from the flooding of their tents.”

“We cannot face the consequences of this storm on our own,” Bassal added.

articles.title: 'No business being in NATO': Presidential hopeful Melenchon pitches radical new course for France
articles.summary: French presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Melenchon on Saturday pledged an economic stimulus programme, including price controls, higher minimum wages and
articles.body: French presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Melenchon on Saturday pledged an economic stimulus programme, including price controls, higher minimum wages and increased taxes on the wealthy, while renewing his call for France to withdraw from NATO. The 75-year-old leader of the left-wing France Unbowed (LFI) party unveiled his 2027 presidential programme at a rally in Le Bourget, near Paris, outlining plans to reverse President Emmanuel Macron's economic policies."We are going to do exactly the opposite — that is to say, a policy of stimulus," Melenchon told supporters at the rally, which drew around 17,000 people, according to his campaign director Manuel Bompard.He said the proposed stimulus would focus on boosting consumer spending and directing existing savings towards social and environmental needs."We have no business being in NATO, nor in American wars," Melenchon said, reiterating his opposition to France's membership of the military alliance. His programme calls for a gradual withdrawal, beginning with an exit from NATO's integrated military command. He also proposed building "a global front of non-aligned countries".Economic and welfare promisesMelenchon's programme, titled "L'Avenir en commun" (A Shared Future), promises measures to tackle the cost-of-living crisis. These include freezing prices, raising the minimum wage and linking wages to inflation.The party wants to increase the net monthly minimum wage to 1,700 euros from around 1,480 euros. It has also proposed capping prices of essential food items, scrapping the flat tax on capital income and increasing taxes on the wealthiest households.The manifesto also promises to reverse Macron's pension reform, which gradually increased the minimum retirement age from 62 to 64 to strengthen public finances. Melenchon wants to restore retirement at 60 for people who have contributed to the pension system for 40 years.Nuclear energy and EU policyOn energy, LFI has reiterated its support for gradually phasing out nuclear power and moving towards an electricity system powered entirely by renewable sources.The programme proposes scrapping the planned EPR2 nuclear reactor programme and ruling out extensions to the operating lives of nuclear plants beyond 60 years.It also criticises Germany's influence over European Union economic policy. The manifesto describes Berlin as the bloc's leading defender of "ordoliberalism", an economic philosophy that emphasises strict budget rules, price stability and independent monetary policy.Melenchon's electoral prospectsMelenchon is seen as the strongest contender on the French left ahead of the 2027 presidential election. Recent opinion polls suggest he could reach the second round in April next year against far-right leader Marine Le Pen.However, the same polls indicate that he could lose to Le Pen in the runoff.The latest manifesto is the fifth edition of LFI's programme. It largely retains policies that have formed the basis of Melenchon's previous presidential campaigns.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Liverpool traders 'priced out' of £12,000 Christmas market pitches
articles.summary: Stall holders said they'd met the council leader to express their concerns at high costs since a new operator took over.
articles.body:
Traders claim they have been priced out of this year's Christmas market.

They have told Liverpool City Council leader Liam Robinson that they cannot afford to take space at the event now that a new operator has taken over running it.

Anthony Grice said he had been quoted £12,000 to take a stall at the St George's Plateau attraction.

Robinson said he had met business owners to "understand the challenges and the issues that they might have had this year" so the authority could look at different options in future.

He said the council had been aware of the price structure being offered to traders by the new operator, Underbelly, when it won the contract to run the event.

And he added that the council would get a share of some of the income.

But Grice said it felt like local traders' concerns were being "swept under the carpet" during a meeting to discuss the plans.

He said: "I asked how many local traders had signed up, and the council didn't know".

He added: "These markets should be a chance to showcase the best of what you've got, but not having the 'Scouse soul' there is so annoying.

Jeweller Alex Healy, from Gateacre, rang a BBC Radio Merseyside phone-in to tell Robinson that she would not be returning to the market this year, despite having been a trader at previous markets since 2021.

She said "It would cost me in the region of £14,000 to £15,000. I have the smallest hut available, but that price I physically cannot afford it."

She said she was acutely aware of the cost-of-living crisis facing her customers, adding: "I don't want to raise my prices. I shouldn't have to."

Robinson said he wanted entrepreneurs like Healy to succeed and invited her to meet him to look at ways the council could support her business.

He added Underbelly had won the tender to run the market "on quality and price" and had a "track record of delivering these markets successfully in lots of other places across the country".

Underbelly has been contacted for comment.

The leader of the Liberal Democrat opposition group on the council, Carl Cashman, said £14,000 was "a rip-off".

He added: "Small businesses are feeling the pinch at the moment, with rising business rates, inflation, and payroll costs, and consumers spending less.

"So £14,000 is just a risk too big for them to take, and the market won't be as good for it."

A Liverpool city council spokesperson said local traders would be able to sell artisan goods at a street market on Basnett Street running on each Saturday in November, plus at regular and pop-up markets in Lark Lane and Woolton Village in the run-up to Christmas.

articles.title: A Florida man sold his Georgia home, put the proceeds in a joint account and used the money to build a house with his wife; after she filed for divorce, an appeals court ruled the down payment was marital property
articles.summary: Money earned or acquired before marriage may remain separate property, but putting it into a joint account can change its legal status.
articles.body: Money earned or acquired before marriage may remain separate property, but putting it into a joint account can change its legal status. This became the central issue in a Florida divorce dispute involving a man who sold his Georgia home after marrying and used the proceeds, along with other funds, towards building a new house with his wife. When the marriage ended, he sought credit for the money he had originally contributed, arguing that it came from his separate property. However, the dispute took a different turn when the wife challenged the financial credits awarded to him by the trial court.In a November 4, 2026, opinion in Anderson v. Anderson, case number 2D2025-1747, the Florida Second District Court of Appeal ruled that the money used for the house's down payment had become marital property after being deposited into a joint bank account and used to finance a jointly titled home. The court reversed the portion of the divorce judgment that had awarded the husband credit for the down payment but upheld his right to receive credit for certain housing expenses he paid after separation. The ruling, available on Justia, sent the case back to the trial court for recalculation of the couple's financial settlement.How the dispute over the house beganThe case involved Melyza C Anderson and Leland A Anderson, whose marriage lasted approximately two years. Before meeting Melyza, Leland owned a house in Georgia. After the couple married, they decided to relocate to Florida and build a home in Tampa.Leland sold his Georgia property and deposited the proceeds into a joint bank account held by the couple. He also transferred a lump sum of money he had earned through his employment into the same account. The couple used money from this account to make a down payment towards constructing their new house. The property was registered in both their names. Shortly after the house was completed, Melyza filed for divorce. Leland moved out but continued paying the monthly mortgage instalments and other expenses associated with the property for the next two years, leading up to the trial.Although Melyza continued living in the house, she did not contribute towards its mortgage payments or maintenance costs. During the divorce proceedings, Leland asked the court to give him financial credit for both the original down payment and the housing expenses he had paid after moving out.Melyza challenged both requests. She argued that the money from the Georgia property had become marital funds because Leland deposited it into their joint account and used it towards a home owned by both spouses. She also argued that his subsequent payments should be treated as temporary support rather than expenses for which he deserved reimbursement.Why the trial court's decision was challengedThe trial court granted Leland credit for the down payment as well as the housing expenses he had covered during the separation. Melyza appealed, arguing that the court had incorrectly treated the original contribution as his separate property. The appeals court examined Florida's rules governing marital and nonmarital assets. Under Florida law, property acquired separately by either spouse can remain nonmarital. However, separately owned assets can lose that status when they are mixed with marital funds.The court explained that money deposited into a joint bank account creates a rebuttable presumption that the depositing spouse intended to give the other spouse an undivided one-half interest in the funds. The spouse seeking to retain the money's separate status must overcome this presumption through clear and convincing evidence.In this case, Leland could not meet that requirement. The court noted that he had deposited the proceeds from his Georgia home into a joint account, mixed them with other funds and then used the money towards a property titled in both spouses' names. The evidence therefore supported treating the down payment as marital property rather than his separate contribution.Why the husband retained credit for other expensesThe appeals court reached a different conclusion regarding the mortgage and maintenance payments Leland made after moving out. It noted that he had continued paying the home's expenses for two years while Melyza lived there without contributing financially. The trial court had found that Melyza had sufficient income to contribute towards the property's upkeep and had not proved a need for temporary support. The appeals court found that this conclusion was supported by the evidence.It also referred to earlier Florida decisions recognising that reimbursement for marital property-related expenses paid by one spouse during separation depends on the circumstances of each case. Consequently, the appeals court reversed the financial credit awarded for the down payment but upheld the credit for the expenses Leland had paid after separation. It remanded the case to the trial court to recalculate the couple's equitable distribution, affirming the divorce judgment in all other respects.The decision highlights how the handling of premarital money can affect property division during divorce. Even when funds originally come from a home owned by one spouse before marriage, transferring them into a joint account and using them for jointly titled property can change their legal character.You use AI every day. articles.title: Weekly round-up: Five stories you may have missed
articles.summary: A phallic-shaped flight path and a rhinos' birthday party feature in our most-read stories this week.
articles.body:
Rhino siblings celebrate first birthday with cake

Two rhino calves have celebrated their first birthday with cakes made of pellets, carrots and salad leaves.

Siblings Markus and Mo were born at Cotswold Wildlife Park, near Burford, last year.

The pair weighed about 70kg (11st) at birth, and now weigh about 500kg (78st) each. Their arrival took the number of rhinos at the park to nine, the most in its 56-year history.

White rhinos were close to extinction in the early 1900s, with fewer than 50 thought to remain in Africa. They are now the most numerous of the five rhino species, but the park says conservation remains vital.

'Surreal' for singer to hear songs on Celebrity Traitors

"I love murder mystery and binge watched with my partner and I'm absolutely hooked, I love it."

The latest series of Celebrity Traitors had its fair share of dramatic moments and shock reveals, but its soundtrack has done much to create the moody atmosphere, with its brooding covers and cinematic compositions.

Dorset singer-songwriter Lloren, real name Lauren Bannon, has had three of her songs featured during some of series two's most explosive moments.

"It was only this series that I was like 'Do you know what, I need to watch this' because... I thought this, this sounds like a bit of me," she said in the countdown to the show's explosive finale on 30 October.

Similar solar farm plans to boost councils' coffers

Two neighbouring councils are aiming to generate green energy and money to fund local services by building and running their own large solar farms .

Work begins next week to install 43,000 solar panels on fields that Wokingham Borough Council owns in the village of Barkham.

West Berkshire Council said construction would begin at its site near Grazeley in March, with plans for 35,000 panels.

The schemes are not connected but are just a few miles apart, and are expected to be operational by the end of 2027.

Firefighters tackle pub kitchen fire on high street

Fire crews have been battling a fire in a pub kitchen on the Isle of Wight .

Hampshire & Isle of Wight Fire & Rescue Service was called to the incident at gastropub The Pier View on the High Street in Cowes on Monday. Black smoke was seen rising from a building in the area.

Crew members could be seen emerging from the next door property with rescued animals, including two cats and a guinea pig, as well as oxygen tanks on their backs.

Firefighters have been using a crane to monitor the situation from above.

Police air service denies penis flight path was deliberate

The service that provides air support to the police has denied deliberately drawing a penis-like shape in the sky via a helicopter's flight path .

Gordon Bird, 53, who lives in Ancells Farm, in Fleet, Hampshire, said his two-year-old daughter was woken up at about 23:00 GMT on Monday by a helicopter flying overhead in multiple circles for at least 15 minutes.

He said he was "shocked" after checking its tracking data online and discovering the phallic shape.

articles.title: We face paying £9,000 tax because our second home is in a war zone
articles.summary: A Ukrainian woman who fled to Scotland is told she and her partner could face a £9,000 property tax charge because she still owns a flat in Kyiv.
articles.body:
A Ukrainian woman who fled to Scotland after Russia invaded her homeland has been told she could face a £9,000 property tax charge because she still owns a flat in Kyiv.

Kateryna Stepanovych, 38, discovered the potential charge when she tried to buy a house in North Ayrshire with her Scottish partner Mattias Lindgren.

The couple were told the Additional Dwelling Supplement (ADS) charge would apply because she already owned a property overseas.

Kateryna bought the small flat in 2018, before Russia's invasion. She fled the war zone in 2023, leaving the property behind.

The conflict has seen shrapnel strike the front of her 10-storey apartment building, damaging its exterior and a neighbouring property. Her own flat remained undamaged.

"The fact that the property is still there is a miracle," Mattias said.

The couple, who currently live in Stromness in Orkney, only became aware of the £9,000 charge when they put down an offer on the property they were planning to buy and Mattias looked through the paperwork from their solicitor.

Unable to afford the additional cost, they had to withdraw their offer.

Mattias said: "Why should we be punished with this tax for a property that's in a war zone?"

Under Revenue Scotland's rules, the Additional Dwelling Supplement Charge can see house buyers facing an additional 8% charge if they already own another property, including overseas.

It was introduced by the Scottish government primarily to target people who are buying second or buy-to-let homes and is paid in addition to Land and Buildings Transaction Tax.

The couple got in touch with Orkney MSP Liam McArthur in the summer after being told by their solicitors there was nothing they could do about the charge.

McArthur then contacted Deputy First Minister Jenny Gilruth, who responded with a letter which stated that there are "no provisions within the legislation that allow either the Scottish government or Revenue Scotland to disapply ADS on a discretionary or case-by-case basis."

Lib Dem MSP McArthur raised the couple's case in the Scottish Parliament on Tuesday, when he asked First Minister John Swinney whether he "agrees with me that this is surely not the intended purpose of the tax?"

Swinney said he would ask Revenue Scotland to investigate the case, adding that he could understand why the rules had created the situation the couple were facing.

Kateryna and Mattias had hoped to relocate this year, but are now considering renting while postponing their plans to buy.

"It's been quite hard because we've had to rethink how we're approaching buying a property," Mattias said.

Kateryna, who works in a factory, has found dealing with the issue particularly challenging because English is not her first language.

"For me, it's difficult," she said, adding there was little else she could do beyond providing documents from Ukraine.

The couple said they are now "biding our time" while exploring their options.

articles.body: The US Central Command (Centcom) on Saturday released a video showing a commercial vessel being struck in what it described as the Gulf of Oman, after US forces disabled a St Kitts-flagged ship that allegedly ignored repeated warnings and attempted to leave the region after visiting an Iranian port. The disclosure came amid heightened tensions between Washington and Tehran and fresh efforts by mediators to revive negotiations to end the conflict.Centcom said the vessel was disabled after it failed to comply with multiple warnings. The US military has been enforcing a naval blockade on Iranian ports for months, including in waters around the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil shipments."CENTCOM forces disabled a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman, Nov. 7, after the ship’s civilian crew ignored repeated warnings and attempted to violate the naval blockade against Iran multiple times. A U.S. military aircraft fired precision munitions at the stern of St. Kitts-flagged M/V Huda, disabling the ship after CENTCOM forces directed the crew to abandon targeted spaces. The cargo vessel tried to depart regional waters after visiting an Iranian port," it said.The latest disclosure comes nearly a month after the last confirmed US strike on a cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman. It also follows at least two reported instances in which Centcom did not publicly acknowledge military strikes in the region. Officials at the command had declined to confirm reports of explosions when questioned about them.Meanwhile, Iranian state media reported explosions on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz and at the port of Jask on Saturday evening. The cause of the explosions was not immediately clear. The US military did not immediately respond to an Associated Press request for comment.Iran's military also said late Saturday that two tankers had struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz area and caught fire. It did not identify the vessels' flags or destinations.Trump confirms fresh US strikesThe latest maritime incident comes days after US President Donald Trump confirmed that American forces had carried out fresh, limited strikes against Iran.Trump said on Friday that the US military had targeted an Iranian air defence system. Describing the action to reporters as “minor”, he confirmed the strikes. However, Centcom did not comment on the operation, even after Trump's remarks.For weeks, Trump had said he was considering a fresh wave of strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections on November 3. The possibility of a return to full-scale military operations has raised concerns across the Middle East and beyond. The US had not resumed such operations since the pause in fighting nearly two months ago.Qatar pushes two-day bridge dealEven as military tensions persist, diplomatic efforts are continuing to find a way out of the conflict.Two Middle Eastern government officials said on Friday that Iran was reviewing proposals presented by Qatar, the chief mediator, to address differences with Washington over Tehran's nuclear programme.Regional officials said the proposal envisages a two-day arrangement involving confidence-building measures by both sides. On the first day, the US would lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports and release some of the billions of dollars in Iranian assets frozen under sanctions.In return, Tehran would allow International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) inspectors to access nuclear sites bombed by the US and Israel.On the second day, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz under a modified arrangement it has reached with Oman. The proposal has not yet received US approval. The arrangement would remain temporary until a permanent agreement on the waterway is reached with other Gulf countries.Once these measures are implemented, Washington and Tehran would begin broader negotiations on Iran's stockpile of highly enriched uranium and other aspects of its nuclear programme, the officials said.However, one of the officials said Iran was currently unwilling to negotiate its nuclear activities until Washington agrees to several conditions that Tehran wants included in any ceasefire agreement.These include an end to the US blockade of Iranian ports, the lifting of sanctions, the release of frozen assets, compensation for war damage and an end to hostilities across the region, including Israeli military operations in Lebanon.The officials spoke on condition of anonymity as they were not authorised to comment publicly on the negotiations.Nuclear programme remains key sticking pointDifferences over Iran's nuclear programme remain the biggest obstacle to a broader agreement. Trump has insisted that the issue must be resolved as part of any deal to end the more than eight-month-old conflict.Iran has consistently maintained that its nuclear programme is intended for peaceful purposes. articles.title: As AI data centres guzzle energy, can we harness their wasted heat?
articles.summary: The rapid development of AI is draining our resources, but engineers have found a way to use heat lost to the air.
articles.body:
As the rapid growth of AI data centres compounds the world’s energy crisis, engineers in Denmark have found a way to make use of the vast amounts of “waste heat” generated by these centres, which is usually lost to the outside air.

There are more than 12,500 data centres around the world and more are coming online every day, straining global energy infrastructure and resources.

Beyond consuming hundreds of billions of litres of water, these systems not only place a massive demand on the global electrical grid, but are likely to be contributing to global warming on a massive scale as well.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) has reported that, in 2024, data centres used 485 terawatt hours of electricity, the equivalent of 1.5 percent of the world’s total energy supply – or the total electricity generation of Germany.

And this figure will double to 3 percent by 2030, with an exponentially growing proportion driven by AI development. This comes as nations are seeking energy independence and need to drastically cut their CO2 emissions.

Indeed, the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe has warned that the rapid expansion of AI hyperscalers – the large-scale cloud service providers like Google, Amazon and Microsoft – and the vast data centres required to support them – pose a “growing threat to electricity systems worldwide”.

The proliferation of data centres is causing widespread anger. In the Netherlands, police arrested protesters against the construction of a new Microsoft data centre close to Amsterdam on Friday. Meanwhile, Elon Musk has earned the ire of residents of Texas, where he moved his AI and SpaceX operations to take advantage of tax breaks. Texans voted in their first Democratic senator – James Talarico – in nearly 40 years in this week’s midterm elections despite Musk sinking hundreds of millions of dollars into campaigns for the Republican Party.

The Bitten supercomputer, which was launched in May this year at the University of Southern Denmark in Sonderborg, is the go-to AI resource for academic research across the country. It provides the AI computing power required for deep data analysis and complex scientific simulations.

But like supercomputers and AI data centres everywhere, Bitten’s capability matches its power consumption. Twenty-four hours a day, its specialised processors generate extreme amounts of thermal energy as they handle the workload.

Now, instead of just allowing that energy to dissipate like AI centres elsewhere, 100 percent of the waste heat is recovered by advanced liquid cooling technology designed by the Danish engineering company Danfoss. This replaces traditional air conditioning and fans that vent to the outside air.

The new system pumps coolant directly over the high-temperature processing chips, completely absorbing the waste heat. That heat can then be channelled directly into Sonderborg’s municipal district heating network to help the town’s 75,000 residents stay warm.

Kristian Strand, president of Danfoss Climate Solutions, told Al Jazeera that whenever we take a picture or upload a document, we activate processing in a data centre.

“That creates heat which we have to remove,” he said. “With the waste heat recovery system, at the end of the process you basically have a tap of hot water coming out of the data centre. That hot water can then be used not only to heat homes but in industrial processes, too.”

Turning data centres into energy sources

Across the world, a colossal amount of energy from industrial processes just vanishes into the atmosphere. Strand told Al Jazeera that Danfoss calculated heat wasted across Europe in one year could power the entire city of Paris for 48 years, while roughly two-thirds of the world’s energy is expelled as excess heat.

The United States hosts more data centres than any other country by far, currently about 4,000. They draw down 5 percent of the nation’s electricity. Yet the US recovers very little heat because it has nowhere to go.

“We should be building data centres where their heat can be used, not just where land is cheapest,” said Jan Rosenow, professor of energy and climate policy at the University of Oxford.

Scandinavia has been leading the way on capturing waste heat, Rosenow said. “Meta’s data centre in Odense in Denmark recovers around 100 GWh a year, enough for 6,900 homes. And Stockholm in Sweden has been feeding data centre heat into its network since 2014.”

At Danfoss, other potential sources of waste heat are being showcased, from supermarket fridge systems, to factories and wastewater treatment plants.

Its engineers recently replaced two carbon-intensive gas boilers at Sonderborg Hospital with a heat pump system that captures waste heat from medical equipment like MRI scanners, and from temperature regulation systems in operating theatres, wards and corridors.

This heat used to be vented outside via cooling towers. Now, the hospital is energy independent for nine months of the year and can feed heat back into the district heating network, saving significant sums on heating bills.

“There was a very good business case for making this happen,” said Lasse Bo Madsen, head of technical services at Sonderborg Hospital. “The project will pay for itself inside two years, and it means we will be able to spend more money on patient care and new equipment, like scanners.”

According to Kristin Strand, this technology is a huge opportunity to save energy and reduce carbon emissions. “We have a vast untapped source of energy in waste heat,” Strand said. “Putting that energy to use reduces reliance on fossil fuels while also making business sense.”

As the AI boom accelerates and new data centres come online, each demanding enough electricity to power a small city, Danfoss believes the scalability of this new waste-heat technology could help ease the soaring demand that is currently stretching global supply.

articles.title: Mapping how France’s protest wave spread across Europe
articles.summary: More than 1,700 cost-of-living demonstrations have hit 31 European countries since mid-September, led by France.
articles.body:
France’s protest movement is showing little sign of easing, nearly two months after high school students first walked out over crumbling classrooms.

On Saturday , 146,000 people rallied across the country, including 46,000 in Paris, according to the Ministry of the Interior, while unions put the figures at 250,000 and 75,000.

Turnout was down from previous weeks, but police used tear gas and batons on protesters in Paris and fired tear gas canisters at hundreds of people blocking a road in central Lyon, France’s third-largest city. About 70,000 security personnel were deployed, days after an estimated 575,000 people joined a union-organised rally.

The protests have expanded to cover a range of issues, from high fuel prices to wages and social housing, and in some cases, the demonstrations have been marred by looting and violence. Police have been accused of using excessive force, with officers using barricades, tear gas and batons against protesters.

Al Jazeera maps where demonstrations, including riots, have taken place across Europe.

An analysis of data from Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) found that between September 15 and October 30, more than 1,200 protests and riots of 100 or more people took place across France over education, public services and the cost of living.

The movement began in mid-September in high schools, where students complained of overcrowded classrooms, a lack of teachers and crumbling buildings. It soon broadened into protests against the rising cost of living, drawing in trade unions and the “yellow vests” movement, with rioting and looting on the sidelines.

On October 17 alone, more than 500,000 people protested nationwide, according to government estimates.

ACLED CEO Clionadh Raleigh said on October 19 that ACLED had recorded an average of 20.5 demonstrations a day in France over the past five years. “During the current protest cycle, that has jumped to almost 66 a day, more than three times the usual rate,” she said.

Protest cycles typically last about 20 days, or 36 for major movements, Raleigh said. By ACLED’s count, this one had reached 45 days and was still going.

“But the most striking difference is the level of confrontation,” she said. “Almost a quarter of events, 24.2 percent, have been classified as riots, compared to a median of just 1.9 percent in previous cycles. Only the unrest following the death of Nahel Merzouk in 2023 recorded a higher proportion.”

The police response has also drawn criticism. On October 28, four United Nations experts mandated by the Human Rights Council expressed alarm at the “excessive use of force” by French authorities in dispersing the student protests.

“The scale of the arrests and detention, affecting several thousand people, mainly minors, appears disproportionate and deters demonstrators from exercising their freedoms of expression and peaceful assembly,” they said in a statement .

In the northern city of Lille, a teenager lost a hand when a grenade exploded as school protesters clashed with police.

France is not protesting alone. Since mid-September, demonstrations over rising living costs, low wages and a lack of public services have broken out in 30 other European countries, from Portugal to Poland.

Between September 15 and October 30, more than 1,700 protests and riots of 100 or more people took place across Europe, according to an analysis of ACLED data.

Although protests in other countries did not reach the same scale as the rallies in France, they may be a sign of discontent spilling over, Alberto Alemanno, professor of European Union law and policy at HEC Paris Business School, told Al Jazeera last month.

“France is the epicentre of this movement … and there are signs now that this is spreading beyond France,” Alemanno said.

France has led the demonstrations, but protests have also broken out across Europe at the same time, driven by a common thread of underfunded education, rising living costs and unaffordable housing.

According to an analysis of ACLED data, France saw more than 1,200 protests and riots between September 15 and October 30, followed by Spain (173), Italy (160), Germany (70) and Portugal (33).

In Spain, tens of thousands of people rallied in early October after parliament rejected two emergency housing decrees on October 2, dealing a blow to Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s minority government.

In Italy, demonstrations over the cost-of-living crisis and unaffordable housing have led to clashes with police.

In Portugal, tens of thousands of protesters marched against the cost-of-living crisis, low wages and an inability to access housing in major cities.

A police officer throws a tear gas canister at a protester during a demonstration against rising living costs in Rennes, France, October 24, 2026 [Jeremias Gonzalez/AP Photo]

Demonstrators clash with police during an antigovernment protest organised by the Italia in Piazza movement, in Milan, October 17, 2026. articles.title: Will Seddon Park provide another bowler-friendly track? Exploring pitch condition in Hamilton before NZ vs IND 3rd ODI
articles.summary: Will Seddon Park offer another bowler-friendly track? Explore the Hamilton pitch report for IND vs NZ 3rd ODI.
articles.body:
Groundsman Karl Johnson says wet weather has made pitch preparation at Seddon Park difficult.

Fast bowlers ruled both ODIs, and New Zealand never lasted beyond 41 overs.

A more balanced surface is expected, though more rain could keep seamers interested.

Seddon Park pitch report for IND vs NZ 3rd ODI: Batting track or bowlers' paradise in Hamilton?

Another bowler-friendly track at Seddon Park is a real possibility, but the final answer may depend as much on the clouds over Hamilton as on the strip itself.

The third ODI between New Zealand and India is scheduled for Tuesday, 10 November, with the first ball due at 3:00 PM local time (NZDT), which is 7:30 AM in India.

India lead the five-match series 2-0, and both wins came on pitches that suited the fast bowlers. The first two ODIs were played at the same venues as the T20Is, and on the same strips, and they produced a very different type of cricket. New Zealand were sent in twice and were unable to bat out 41 overs on either occasion, as the ball moved off the seam and the bounce was steep and at times uneven.

At Seddon Park, head groundsman Karl Johnson is working through a difficult build-up. A tractor-mounted machine called a verti-drain has been rumbling over the outfield, punching holes into the grass with its tines so that the ground gets more air and drains faster if the rain returns, as more rain is expected on Monday and Tuesday.

The early expectation is for a more balanced surface than the ones seen in Auckland and Wellington, although the weather could still keep the seamers interested.

Seddon Park groundsman Karl Johnson on pitch preparation for IND vs NZ 3rd ODI

According to Johnson, an unusually wet start to November across New Zealand is probably the biggest reason why the pitches have behaved the way they have this series.

The T20Is before the ODIs were high-scoring affairs, with New Zealand making a record 259 at Eden Park and India chasing 199 in only 13.2 overs at Hnry Stadium in Wellington. The ODIs, in contrast, were low-scoring and dominated by the bowlers.

He said the aim is to prepare a surface that stays consistent for 100 overs with minimal seam movement, but the unsettled conditions have made that harder.

"New Zealand's been pretty wet over the last few days, and we've had quite a lot of rain here yesterday, so we've lost out some time but we've been able to get the pitch ready," he said in an interview wth Cricinfo.

The groundsman then talked about the forecast and the steps taken to speed up preparation, since a pitch kept under covers for long periods tends to sweat.

"Good day today, beautiful day today, Sunday, matchday minus two," Johnson said. "Forecast isn't great for tomorrow and matchday is not flash either, so we're trying to fast-track our pitch, because when they sit under our covers, they do sweat a bit."

He also expects the covers to be on for large parts of the next two days, which will limit what his staff can do. "Tomorrow probably looks like half a day," Johnson said. "We might be okay in the morning, we might lose out in the afternoon. And then matchday looks a bit challenging as well."

Johnson added that the weather is changing quickly because of the storms moving through, which makes it hard to plan around specific hours. "It's difficult to pinpoint it down to time and stuff," he said. "So we're just trying to do a whole lot today."

Seddon Park pitch report: Pace, seam, spin and batting conditions in Hamilton

Seddon Park has compact square boundaries of roughly 60 to 65 metres, and the longer straight hits have tempted stroke-makers for years. The average first-innings score in ODIs at the ground is between 240 and 245, and the venue is known for high scores when the surface is dry. Overcast skies, however, bring early seam movement into play.

The pitch is different from the steep, spongy bounce of Eden Park or the damp surface in Wellington. With the new ball and under humid skies, Seddon Park usually gives the bowlers some lateral movement at the start, but once the first 10 to 12 overs have been negotiated, the bounce becomes truer and horizontal-bat shots are easier to play.

Wrist-spinners and defensive finger-spinners can find some grip in the middle overs if the surface stays dry, although the short square boundaries punish small errors in line and length. Chasing sides have enjoyed a slight edge at the venue, particularly when early moisture dries out, and rain interruptions bring DLS calculations into play.

Hamilton weather forecast for IND vs NZ 3rd ODI at Seddon Park: Temperature, wind and humidity

The temperature is expected to stay between 16 and 18 degrees Celsius through the afternoon and evening, although the RealFeel figure is likely to be considerably lower, dropping from about 16 degrees at 1:00 PM to between 12 and 13 degrees late at night.

A north-easterly wind of roughly 22 km/h is forecast during the afternoon, easing to about 15 km/h by 11:00 PM, while gusts could reach as high as 46 km/h in the early part of the match window.

Weather, not the pitch, may decide the third ODI at Seddon Park

On paper, Seddon Park looks like the friendliest ground of the series for batters. The boundaries are short, the bounce usually becomes true after the new ball loses its shine, and the venue's first-innings average is a healthy 240 to 245. A surface of that type would be a welcome change for a New Zealand batting line-up that has been bundled out cheaply twice.

The trouble is that very little about this week has been normal. Johnson's covers are likely to be on for long stretches, and a pitch that sits under plastic tends to sweat, which usually helps the bowlers in the first hour. With heavy rain forecast around the toss, the team that bowls first could therefore find early assistance even on a surface that was meant to be flat.

That also makes the toss more interesting than the history suggests. A chasing side gets the benefit of any DLS calculation, and any restart would give the target-setting team less certainty about what a good score is. India, who are 2-0 up, could decide to field again, whereas New Zealand will either need to win the toss or bat well to stay in the series.

Whatever the pitch offers, the first hour is likely to be the most important. If the batters survive it, Hamilton could finally give them a game.

articles.title: Massachusetts neighbours spent years complaining about sand, dust and noise from an adjoining mine; in August 2026, a jury awarded the couple $530,000 after finding the operators liable for property impacts
articles.summary: A Massachusetts couple who spent years dealing with dust, noise and vibrations from a neighbouring sand mining operation have won $530,000 in damages
articles.body: A Massachusetts couple who spent years dealing with dust, noise and vibrations from a neighbouring sand mining operation have won $530,000 in damages after a jury found the operators liable for the impact on their property. The verdict, delivered on August 11, 2026, in Plymouth Superior Court, followed a lengthy legal battle involving complaints about airborne sand, heavy truck traffic and potential exposure to silica dust. Details of the case were reported by the Community Land & Water Coalition, with further coverage from the Plymouth Independent and legal publication Exlitem. Josephine and Keith Beadling brought the case against G. Lopes Construction Inc. and landowner Bette Maki, whose property at 0 Meadow Street in Carver, Massachusetts, was used for sand and gravel extraction. The mining operation had continued for more than a decade, with the couple raising concerns about its effects on their home and surrounding neighbourhood. According to the trial findings, the jury held both G. Lopes Construction and Maki liable for private nuisance, finding that their involvement in the operation substantially and unreasonably interfered with the couple's use and enjoyment of their property. Responsibility for this claim was divided, with 80% assigned to the construction company and 20% to the landowner.The verdict covered three legal claims: Nuisance, negligence and negligent trespass. Under the negligent-trespass claim, the jury awarded the couple $200,000 each for pain and suffering, along with $15,000 each for property damage. A further $100,000 was awarded under the negligence claim, bringing the total damages to $530,000. With mandatory interest, the amount is expected to exceed $760,000.The scale of the mining activity was a significant part of the case. Evidence presented during the trial indicated that the operation generated at least 54,000 truck trips over its 13-year run, with heavy vehicles passing within approximately 35 feet of the couple's front door. On some days, the number of trips reportedly reached 120. Residents described persistent noise, vibrations and dust accumulating on their cars, outdoor spaces and other parts of their properties.The trial also examined the potential health implications of the dust. Environmental engineering expert Scott Hersey presented laboratory findings identifying respirable crystalline silica in samples collected from the mining site. His analysis of more than a million weather observations found that winds had travelled from the mine towards the couple's home before 20 of 25 documented dust incidents.Pulmonary specialist Stephen L. Newman also testified about the residents' respiratory complaints and the possible effects of prolonged silica exposure. His assessment raised concerns about potential silica-related lung complications. However, neither resident received a confirmed diagnosis of silicosis, and the medical testimony should not be confused with a diagnosis delivered by the jury.The couple's legal battle had begun well before the trial. They had reportedly brought complaints about the mining activity to Carver town officials as early as 2014, raising concerns about dust, excessive truck traffic, noise and vibrations. Their lawsuit was filed in April 2023, challenging the operation and seeking relief over its impact on neighbouring properties. An attempt to secure an injunction to stop the excavation while the case was pending was rejected by a Superior Court judge in July 2023. The operation continued until March 2024, despite further objections from residents and legal proceedings surrounding the permits.The case has also drawn attention beyond Carver, where sand and gravel extraction has become a wider environmental and community concern. A separate report by the New Bedford Light in April 2026 examined how large-scale excavation in southeastern Massachusetts affects nearby residents, particularly through dust emissions and concerns about groundwater resources. The Plymouth Independent subsequently highlighted the Beadling verdict as an important development for communities dealing with similar mining disputes.The Meadow Street operation involved excavation across approximately 19 acres, with experts also examining its proximity to the Plymouth-Carver Sole Source Aquifer, an important regional drinking water resource. The case has brought renewed attention to the effects of commercial sand extraction on residential neighbourhoods and the responsibility of operators to prevent their activities from affecting neighbouring properties.You use AI every day. articles.title: What happens if all the lights go out? This is the plan for a 'Black Sky' event
articles.summary: How prepared is the UK for the type of event that could leave millions without power, water and communications?
articles.body:
It was a Saturday night in early December when Roger Kemp realised something was very wrong.

"I was halfway through a Scandi crime drama when everything went off," the professor at Lancaster University told the BBC. "Streetlights were off. The sodium glow that we can see over the horizon from Morecambe was off."

"[It was] almost like a zombie movie," he said. "People trying to find phone reception, wondering where things were, and there was a huge queue at the one working telephone box."

At 22:45 on 5 December 2015, the River Lune - which flows directly through Lancaster - had flooded, and the electricity supply to 61,500 people in the city went.

Households lost light and heat, some water supplies also began to fail because they relied on electric pumps. The railway station closed. So too petrol stations and shops. Most cash machines didn't work. Traffic lights failed.

The two communication systems that survived were copper wire landline telephones and FM radio. The local commercial radio station The Bay had an emergency generator and one landline and a reporter was sent outside the affected area to ring in with information.

Three months later, Kemp, a professor of engineering with a specialism in safety and electrical systems, gathered people together to look at everything that had gone wrong.

"It is perhaps ironic that, in a society with huge commitment to digital infrastructure, the most reliable source of news was a commercial station using technology that would have been familiar to the engineers on the 1960s Radio Caroline pirate radio ship," the subsequent report concluded.

For Kemp and others in the field of civil contingency, Lancaster was a warning. When a town loses power for several days, our connected world falls apart. This kind of disruption has been given a name: a Black Sky event.

At a recent summit on UK resilience, the conversation focused on the need for the UK to be able to withstand a Black Sky event for a minimum of 72 hours.

"We are nine meals from anarchy" is a phrase often heard in the civil contingency world. A brutal reminder of the fear that three days without food would be enough to turn a crisis into chaos. If a Black Sky event takes out electricity, water, shops and communications, there is a good reason the government wants us to have our own supplies.

The much talked about "Be Ready" campaign is designed to help ready us for all sorts of possible crises, but the government says there is no specific threat to the grid. Regardless, a Black Sky event is definitely at the backs of people's minds.

In a major emergency, we are being told to hunker down and turn on an FM radio, as thousands did in Lancaster. This is why the BBC has its own Black Sky plan.

Only a small number of staff know the full details, but from what I have gleaned, about 100 people in the BBC will run a special emergency radio studio.

It will have secure lines of communication not dependent on the internet, and fuel, water and food to ensure it can operate without resupply for at least three days.

This emergency service will broadcast pre-arranged government messaging. The scripts have already been published online.

They include instructions on how much people should be drinking each day and how to dispose of toilet waste without flushing the toilet.

Other information will be broadcast via satellite vehicles from a select number of journalists at emergency centres around the UK, which will carry on as long as the diesel lasts.

The BBC's broadcasts will be sent via radio transmission towers, isolated from the internet and equipped with tanks of between five and 40,000 litres (8,800 gallons) of diesel to keep their generators going for three days - FM radio is power hungry. The teams will be using satellite phones to keep in touch and if these stop working there are pre-agreed protocols and meet-up points.

Why FM? Because it works almost everywhere, even in a blackout or a crippling cyber-attack.

"It was originally thought we should plan for five to seven days," I was told quietly by one BBC insider. "The latest advice from Neso [National Energy System Operator] is that they will probably be able to get the power back on in two to three days."

Of course, fears of a grid failure are not new, but recent events such as the mass blackout in Spain, Portugal and south-western France in April 2025 have pushed it up the agenda. And the more it happens, the more it reveals the problems it can create in our networked world.

People need to know power cuts are about more than just the lights going out, says Lord Harris, chair of the UK's National Preparedness Commission. ''It's likely to stop the water supply because unless you happen to be located neatly downstream of a reservoir, that requires electricity," he told me.

More importantly, sewage tends to solidify unless water can move through it, he adds, "and that then causes blockages, the whole thing backs up, you get sewage flowing out, flowing back up the system".

It's common for governments in Europe to regularly advise households to stock up on supplies in case of a national emergency - but the UK is behind in its warnings to the population.

However, work has begun on some backup systems, such as High Altitude Pseudo-Satellites (HAPS). The government-sponsored Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA) is spending £70m developing planes that can circle over the UK and provide at least a week of emergency mobile phone and internet connectivity at times of crisis.

"When ground networks fail, there are limits to what satellites can provide as a fallback," said Rico Chandra, programme director for ARIA's Enduring Atmospheric Platforms.

We live in a complex, electrically powered world - but the more connected everything becomes the more catastrophic it is when that fails.

In the drive towards efficiency over the last five decades, we've lost backup systems, says Lord Harris.

An example of this is the new communication system being adopted by the emergency services, which will replace radio comms with mobile phone network technology, says Lord Harris, "so if the mobile phone goes down it will also impact on emergency services communications".

However, the government insists "moving emergency services onto modern 4G and 5G technologies" is "resilient and reliable".

The Cabinet Office said: "The UK has one of the most resilient electricity systems in the world, and there has never been a complete outage in the grid's 75-year history."

Government enthusiasm for resilience is nothing new. Oliver Dowden, the then deputy prime minister, launched the last Conservative government's disaster planning initiative in May 2024. The launch was somewhat overshadowed by Sunak announcing an election on the same day but, two years on, calls for at least three days of resilience have only grown stronger.

At the beginning of researching this article I spoke to an engineer about the UK's TV and radio transmission masts, their lonely isolation from the rest of the digital landscape sounded like a failing. It now feels like an argument in their favour.

The current urgency for disaster planning is coming at an interesting moment for technology we used to rely on. The UK's copper wire landline system - which would work even in a power cut - will be switched off on 31 January 2027. The future of FM radio is also under government review.

The response from the government was that while copper landlines had been a useful fallback during power cuts, they were now unreliable and difficult to repair.

As I ended my call with Kemp, I asked him if his report had helped improve our readiness for a Black Sky. He paused.

"If anything, we've gone backwards," he said. "Switching off the public switch telephone network, I think shows that there has been really no thought at all about how you communicate when you've no longer got power."

While writing this piece last Saturday I had to break off for an hour because my street was suddenly plunged into darkness. We had a power cut.

I found my emergency torch, but the batteries had leaked. My candles had been pushed to the back of a cupboard and I had no idea where I had put my wind-up radio with its emergency torch.
authors: David Sillito - Media and Arts correspondent

articles.title: Chawri Bazar building collapse: Toll rises to 7
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The death toll in the three-storey building collapse in central Delhi's Chawri Bazar area rose to seven on Sunday after another body was
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The death toll in the three-storey building collapse in central Delhi's Chawri Bazar area rose to seven on Sunday after another body was recovered from the debris.Rescue operations have been underway for more than 70 hours, an official said, news agency PTI reported.The deceased has been identified as Luchhuman Mukhiya, 66, a resident of Darbhanga in Bihar. His body was recovered during the search and rescue operation at the collapsed structure near Chawri Bazar.The mortal remains have been shifted to LNJP Hospital for further proceedings. With the latest recovery, seven bodies have been pulled out of the rubble so far.Rescue personnel are continuing the search for any other possible victims.The building collapsed around 9.48am on November 5 while construction work was underway. The rescue operation has continued for over 70 hours since the incident.The deceased have been identified as Sanjeet Kumar, Kishori Sah, Pankaj Sharma, Vipin Ram, Shantu, Dinesh Sah and Luchhuman Mukhiya. Four of the victims were residents of Bihar, while Vipin Ram lived in Mandawali in Delhi, police said.The building owner, identified as Saimullah alias Ayub, and three contractors, Siraj, Tajuddin and Furkan, have been arrested in connection with the incident.The contractors were apprehended from Faridabad's Sirohi, PTI reported.An FIR was registered at Hauz Qazi police station on November 5 under Sections 105 (culpable homicide not amounting to murder), 290 (negligent conduct with respect to pulling down or repairing buildings), 125(a) (act endangering life or personal safety of others) and 3(5) (common intention) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.The building was allegedly being constructed without the requisite approval on a 50-square-metre plot. articles.title: The anti-Netanyahu: Can Gadi Eisenkot give the world a different Israel?
articles.summary: Unpolished and understated, Eisenkot offers a stark contrast to Netanyahu but risks continuing his legacy
articles.body:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog has tasked the leader of the Yashar (“Straight”) party, Gadi Eisenkot, with assembling a government after elections left no political alliance with a majority in the Knesset.

Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff, will now have 28 days, with the possibility of a 14-day extension, to put together a government before Herzog allows an alternative leader, most likely Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, to try to do the same. If this fails, then new elections would be called.

But as things stand, Eisenkot is unlikely to be able to form a majority government of the kind Netanyahu has relied upon to force through his right-wing policy agenda.

He may have to rely upon the support of at least one of the two parties representing the ultra-Orthodox community, which have often been allies of Netanyahu. It will also be critical for him to persuade some of the more right-wing elements of his opposition bloc to get the support of Arab parties outside the government.

How far he will be able to go in this is uncertain for a man whom observers described as less comfortable with the subterfuge and political guile often attributed to Netanyahu.

Eisenkot emerged as the leader of his volatile opposition bloc just days before the October 27 elections, and even then, messaging from within the coalition appeared confused, contradictory and seemingly absent of any central coordinating figure.

So far, any support from the ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism Party, which has broken with its traditional ally Shas in declining to endorse Netanyahu, is likely to come in return for the continuation of the de facto shield afforded to young ultra-Orthodox men who refuse military service.

Support from parties representing Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, even if offered from outside the government, is likely to come in return for at least some meaningful effort to tackle the violent crime wave that has been allowed to engulf Palestinian communities inside Israel.

They will also want the epidemic of violent settler pogroms , which have swept through the occupied West Bank with the seemingly active encouragement of Netanyahu’s government partners – particularly far-right Ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich – to stop.

But Aida Touma-Sliman, a Knesset member from the left-wing Hadash party and a member of the Palestinian-led Joint List, said developments in recent days showed that Eisenkot doesn’t want to rely on Palestinian voters.

“He appears much more willing to compromise with the ultra-Orthodox religious parties, particularly over the law governing military conscription, than risk being seen to depend on Arab support.”

One of the primary issues that whoever leads the country next will have to deal with is Israel’s standing in the United States. Israel’s reputation has fallen to an all-time low among the American public due to the genocidal war on Gaza and the US-Israel war on Iran, which Netanyahu is accused of convincing US President Donald Trump to start.

On the eve of what turned out to be disastrous midterm elections for Trump, he announced an end to the $3.8bn military aid package extended to Israel annually.

Irrespective of the last-minute announcement, Trump’s Republican Party suffered historic losses, and senior officials, including Vice President JD Vance, blamed the war on Iran.

Carnegie Endowment senior fellow Aaron David Miller acknowledged Israel’s reputation in the US was at a low ebb, one that Eisenkot – with his discomfort over the public stage and reluctance to speak in English – would need to address.

“Perceptions of Israel are fairly entrenched. Essentially, the public’s been watching the region in split screen since 2023. On one screen, there’s the carnage inflicted by Hamas on October 7 [2023], and on the other, there’s the death and destruction unleashed by Israel in response.”

“In the eyes of many, Israel is no longer David but Goliath,” he told Al Jazeera. “Ahead of Eisenkot may be the toughest US landscape any Israeli prime minister has to navigate.”

For now, at least, Eisenkot has the backing of the majority of Israelis as much for what he isn’t as for what he is.

Unlike Netanyahu, the well-polished son of a privileged Ashkenazi Jewish family who has nevertheless sought to leverage the grievances of Mizrahi Jews, Eisenkot represents a more genuine package.

Born in Tiberias to parents from Marrakesh and Casablanca, he grew up in the equally remote southern port city of Eilat before joining the army at 18, later rising to the rank of chief of staff. He then followed the well-worn path of senior Israeli military officers into politics, eventually serving in the national unity government assembled by Netanyahu after the Hamas- led attacks on southern Israel on October 7, 2023.

Described by both allies and opponents as both “menschy” (decent) and “schlumpy” (unkempt ), Eisenkot’s careworn appearance reflects, at least in the eyes of some voters, his personal connections with the October 7 attacks and subsequent genocidal war on Gaza.

His son Gal was killed in Jabalia in northern Gaza in December 2023 while taking part in the war, followed a day later by his nephew Maor.

In November 2024, another nephew, Yogev Pazy, was killed in Gaza. This has created a persona around Eisenkot at odds with Netanyahu’s family, whose relatively glamorous lifestyle appears far removed from the Israeli public’s current situation.

“He seems very military in his bearing, very steady and a man you don’t always know what he’s thinking,” Yossi Mekelberg, a senior fellow at Chatham House, said. “I think he’s offering what Israel needs above all else right now: a sense of normalcy and the understanding that there are rules that apply equally and to everyone, including the government.”

But this will make little difference for Palestinians. Eisenkot is the architect of the Dahiyeh Doctrine , which advocates the use of disproportionate force and widespread destruction against civilian communities resisting Israeli force. It is far from clear if Eisenkot’s appointment as premier will make any difference to the yawning gulf in rights between Jewish and Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Eisenkot was reported to have expressed resentment at having to sit alongside such far-right figures as Ben-Gvir and Smotrich during his eight-month tenure in the national unity government. But he has nevertheless overseen punishing policies upon both Palestinians and Arabs in neighbouring states.

As chief of staff, Eisenkot oversaw brutal operations against Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank as well as overseeing extensive air strikes against Iranian targets and arming rebels in Syria.

From 2015 to 2018, years overlapping with his tenure, United Nations figures record about 650 Palestinians killed by Israeli forces or in conflict-related incidents. The toll included 295 deaths in 2018 alone. Among them were 189 Palestinians killed and thousands wounded during the Great March of Return protests in Gaza, including 35 children.

A UN commission later found reasonable grounds to believe that Israeli forces under his command had committed serious violations of international law, some potentially amounting to war crimes or crimes against humanity.

During the 2006 war in Lebanon when Eisenkot is credited with having devised the Dahiyeh Doctrine, Israel killed 1,109 people , about 860 of whom were civilians. There are no numbers for the tens of thousands of people killed under Eisenkot’s tactic in the years since.
